assert.short: A line of code that stops a program with a message when a stated condition is false.

balancing.short: Keeping the power that plants make equal to the power that people use, at every moment.

balancing-authority.short: The organisation that keeps supply and demand balanced, moment to moment, in its own part of the grid.

battery-duration.short: How many hours a battery can discharge at its rated power: its energy in MWh divided by its power in MW.

capacity.short: The most power a plant can produce at once, often called its nameplate size.

capacity-factor.short: The energy a plant actually made over a period, divided by the energy it would have made running at full capacity the whole time.

carbon-intensity.short: The CO2 emitted for each unit of electricity, for example in tonnes per megawatt-hour.

combined-cycle.short: A gas power plant that burns gas in a turbine and uses the hot exhaust to make steam for a second turbine, so it gets more electricity from the same fuel.

constraint.short: A rule every solution must obey, such as supply equals demand or no plant above its size.

utc.short: The world reference clock, with no daylight saving; EIA stamps its hourly grid data in it.

counterfactual.short: What would have happened without the change being judged; every saving or effect is measured against one.

curtailment.short: Turning a wind or solar farm below what the weather allows, usually because the grid has more power than it can use at that moment.

dataframe.short: A pandas table with named columns and an index, such as one row per hour.

daylight-saving-time.short: Clocks moved an hour ahead in summer, giving one 23-hour day in spring and one 25-hour day in autumn.

decision-variable.short: A quantity the model is free to choose, such as how much each plant makes each hour.

demand.short: The total power that all users on a grid draw at a given moment.

dispatch.short: Deciding how much power each plant should make, hour by hour or minute by minute.

dispatchable.short: A power plant whose output the operator can turn up or down on request, such as a gas plant.

duck-curve.short: The daily shape of demand minus solar output, with a dip at midday and a steep climb in the evening.

duration-curve.short: A year of hourly values sorted from highest to lowest, showing for how many hours each level is reached.

energy.short: An amount of electricity made or used over a stretch of time, equal to power multiplied by time and measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh) or megawatt-hours (MWh).

energy-storage.short: Equipment, such as a battery, that takes in electricity at one time and gives it back later, with some losses.

evidence-ladder.short: The stages a project climbs: announced, funded, permitted, under construction, operating and at design output.

firm-capacity.short: Power that can be counted on whenever it is needed, whatever the weather.

forecast-error.short: The difference between what was forecast, such as tomorrow's demand or wind, and what actually happened.

frozen-telemetry.short: A measurement feed stuck on its last value, which shows up as the same reading hour after hour.

gigawatt.short: A thousand megawatts, a rate of energy flow used for large plants, whole fleets and national demand.

frequency.short: The number of cycles per second of the grid's alternating current, 60 hertz (Hz) in North America, which falls when power is short and rises when there is too much.

hour-ending.short: A time stamp that labels each hour by its last moment, so 01:00 means the hour from midnight to 01:00.

kilowatt-hour.short: The unit of energy on a household electricity bill: one kilowatt kept up for one hour.

lcoe.short: A plant's lifetime costs divided by the electricity it makes over its life, both discounted to today's money, giving an average cost per megawatt-hour.

linear-program.short: An optimization problem in which the goal and all the rules are linear, so each is a sum of quantities times fixed numbers.

megawatt.short: A unit of power equal to one million watts, or a thousand kilowatts.

megawatt-hour.short: A unit of energy: one megawatt kept up for one hour, or a thousand kilowatt-hours.

merit-order.short: Running power plants in order of their running cost, cheapest first.

objective.short: What an optimization tries to make as small or as large as possible, such as the total cost.

optimization.short: Finding the best choice among many, given a goal and the rules the choice must obey.

pareto-frontier.short: The set of plans that cannot be made cheaper without becoming dirtier, or cleaner without becoming more expensive.

peaker.short: A power plant that runs only in the hours of highest demand, because it starts quickly but is expensive to run.

power.short: How fast electricity is being made or used at a given moment, measured in watts, kilowatts (kW) or megawatts (MW).

projection.short: A model's estimate of a future quantity under stated assumptions, not a measurement or a promise.

ramp-rate.short: How fast a power plant can raise or lower its output, for example in megawatts per minute or per hour.

reactive-power.short: The part of alternating-current power that does no net work but holds voltage up; it is supplied and absorbed locally.

resample.short: Regroup a time series to a coarser step, such as hours to days, by averaging or summing.

reserves.short: Spare capacity that operators keep ready to cover the sudden loss of a plant or a forecast that misses.

round-trip-efficiency.short: The share of the energy put into storage that comes back out.

running-cost.short: What it costs a plant to make one more megawatt-hour, mostly fuel, leaving out the cost of building it.

shadow-price.short: How much the best total cost would change if one rule were loosened by one unit; for the rule that supply equals demand, it is the price of one more megawatt-hour.

solver.short: Software that finds the best solution of an optimization problem, or shows that none exists.

system-boundary.short: The line that decides which parts, costs and emissions a study counts and which it leaves out.

telemetry.short: Measurements sent automatically from plants and substations to the grid operator.

terawatt-hour.short: A billion kilowatt-hours, the usual unit for a year of a country's or a sector's electricity use.

unserved-energy.short: Demand that could not be met, so some customers lost power.

variable-renewables.short: Wind and solar power, whose output follows the weather: they can be turned down but not up.

voltage.short: The electrical pressure that pushes current along a line; grids hold it within a narrow band at every point.

wholesale-price.short: The price at which electricity is traded between power plants and the companies that sell it to customers, often set hour by hour.
